title: Cash register and POS terminal: drawer solenoid, printer motor, screens and cells
summary: A shop till is a cash drawer, a thermal receipt printer, a barcode scanner, a screen and a couple of power bricks. Between them they give a 12–24 V release solenoid, strong ejector springs, a small stepper motor with gears, a red laser diode with its scanning mirror, LCD screens, 12–24 V power supplies and a lithium cell in wireless readers. About 40 minutes with a screwdriver set; the dangers are the spring-loaded drawer, the printer's cutter blade and swollen lithium cells.

steps.text: Unplug everything. Pull the power bricks out of the wall first, then the leads from the terminal, printer and drawer. Lift any wireless card reader or handheld scanner off its dock and set it aside. Lay the pieces out on a bench so you can strip them one at a time.
steps.warn: Some all-in-one terminals have a mains supply inside. If a mains lead goes into the case, unplug it and wait 5 minutes before you open it.

steps.text: Open the cash drawer: use the key, or the manual release lever or cable that most drawers have underneath or at the back. Lift out the cash tray and the coin and note bowls (they make good sorting trays), then slide the drawer fully out of its case and lift it off its slides.
steps.warn: The ejector springs throw the drawer open hard. Keep your face and hands clear of the front as you release it and don't lean over it.

steps.text: Turn the case over and take out the screws in the base. The release solenoid is a small coil with a plunger at the back, linked to a latch lever. Its two wires go to a small board or straight to a phone-style (RJ11 or RJ12) jack. Read the voltage on its label (12 V or 24 V). Unscrew it from its bracket and cut the wires 10 cm long, or take the jack and its cable with it. Keep the latch lever and the plunger return spring.
Now that the drawer is out and the springs are at rest, unhook the ejector springs with pliers and keep them together with the latch.
steps.warn: Hold each spring in the pliers as you unhook the second end. A stretched spring flicks the hook toward your eyes.

steps.text: Receipt printer: open the paper cover, take out the roll and flip up the lever over the print head. Undo the case screws and lift the housing. The paper-feed stepper motor and its small gear train sit beside the rubber roller. Unplug the motor, undo its 2 screws and lift it out with its gears still on the bracket. Take the rubber roller too.
steps.warn: The auto-cutter blade at the paper exit is very sharp. Leave the cutter assembly alone or take it out carefully by its plastic frame.

steps.text: Leave the thermal print head: it is a fragile strip of tiny heating dots with no easy second use.

Barcode scanner with a red scan line: unscrew the housing and lift out the scan engine, a small block holding the laser diode and a mirror on a tiny moving coil. Unplug it and take it whole, with its cable. A scanner with a plain window and a ring of LEDs is camera-based: it has no laser diode, only a small camera board.
steps.warn: Never power a laser scanner with its case open and look into the beam. Don't point the beam at anyone's eyes.

steps.text: Screens: take the customer display and the touchscreen off their stands (screws under the base and behind the neck). Lift the back covers with a plastic pry tool. Keep each panel, its driver board and its backlight lead together as one unit.
steps.warn: Glass. A cracked panel cuts and leaks. Older screens lit by fluorescent tubes hold a little mercury: keep them whole and don't crush them.

steps.text: Power supplies: take the 12 V and 24 V bricks, and the terminal's own supply if it has one, whole with their cables. Read the label (volts, amps, plug polarity) and write the rating on the brick with tape or a marker. Check the output with a multimeter at the plug before you use it.
steps.warn: Don't open a brick. Its capacitors can hold a charge after unplugging.

steps.text: Wireless card readers and handhelds: work the seam open with a plastic pry tool, unplug the battery connector and lift the cell out. Look for swelling, a puffy case or heat. Measure the voltage: about 3.7 V nominal, 4.2 V full.
steps.warn: A swollen or damaged cell goes outdoors on bare ground (see safety_swollen_lithium). Don't pry at a cell or let a tool touch both of its terminals.

steps.text: Coin cell: find the CR2032 in its holder on the terminal's main board and lift it out with a wooden or plastic tool. Check it with the meter: above about 2.8 V it is still fine for a clock or small loads.
Cables: take the USB, serial, drawer (RJ11 or RJ12) and power cables whole with their plugs. Pull on the plug, never the wire. Coil them and label which is which.

notes:
## What's worth keeping and why

- **Drawer solenoid and latch.** A 12 V or 24 V push-pull actuator made for short pulses. Use it for door latches, trap doors, feeder gates or remote catches. Drawer solenoids are rated for a second or so: don't leave one switched on or it will overheat.
- **Ejector springs.** Strong, short springs for latches, return springs and spring-loaded catches.
- **Stepper motor and gears.** A small 24 V stepper with a gear reduction. Use it for a feeder, a dial or a slow winder. It needs a stepper driver and runs at lower torque on lower voltage.
- **Laser diode and scan engine.** A red laser of a few milliwatts. Use it as a pointer, an alignment line or a beam-break sensor. A laser diode needs a current-limited driver, not a battery across it.
- **Screens.** An LCD with its driver board makes a small display for a camera, a computer or a gauge. Many driver boards run from 12 V.
- **Power bricks.** 12 V and 24 V supplies for lights, routers and radios, or for the printer's own motors.
- **Lithium cell and coin cell.** Test each (see test_lithium_cell) before you trust it.

## Opening the drawer without the register

Many drawers fire from a 12 V or 24 V pulse sent by the receipt printer through the RJ jack. A battery of the right voltage and a push button across the solenoid wires will open one. Check the label voltage first; the pulse should be short.

## Variations

- Cheap tills (a keypad with a built-in printer) are a small circuit board, a tiny thermal printer and a drawer solenoid. Strip them the same way.
- All-in-one terminals are small computers (x86 or ARM) with memory and storage. If one still boots, keep it whole.
- Payment-card reader modules carry tamper-protection. They have nothing worth taking beyond the cell and the case.

## What to leave

- The thermal print head, the cutter blade and the card reader module.
- The cash drawer's steel case: heavy, but a good lockable box for tools or papers.
